Welcome to Nanomedicine Fabrication!

Good morning, everyone! Today, we are going to do something incredibly fun and hands-on. Over the last two lectures, we explored various theoretical applications of nanoscience. Now, it is time to step into the shoes of a nanomedicine engineer and actually fabricate a real particle for treatment.

Specifically, we are going to build a controlled release platform. To pull this off, we need to draw on integrated sciences—chemistry, biology, physics, and engineering—just as we do in our broader nanoscience major.

Why do we want to control the release of a drug? Imagine taking a medication that immediately floods your system. It might be too strong at first and then wear off too quickly. By engineering a nanoparticle that mimics sustainable, slow release, we can maintain a perfect, steady dosage in the patient’s body.

The Materials: Biology Meets Chemistry

To build our particle, we need the right building blocks. Today, our primary material is sodium alginate. But where does this material come from?

Sodium alginate is extracted from brown seaweed, specifically from the plant cell walls. Because it comes from a natural plant source, it is food-grade and highly biocompatible. This is a crucial question we must always ask in nanomedicine: Is the material safe for the human body? If we can eat it in boba, it is generally a great candidate for safely delivering drugs inside the body!

Alongside sodium alginate, we will use a salt called calcium chloride (\text{CaCl}_2). Let’s look at what happens when we try to dissolve these two materials in pure water.

If you take the calcium chloride powder and shake it in water, it dissolves almost immediately. But if you try the same thing with the sodium alginate powder, it clumps up and floats on the surface, looking cloudy and stubborn. Why is there such a massive difference in how they dissolve?

The answer lies in their chemical structures. Calcium chloride is made of small molecules that easily separate into ions in water. Sodium alginate is a massive polymer—a long, complex chain of molecules. Because the structure is so large, it takes a significantly longer time for the water molecules to surround and dissolve it.

If you were to stir both powders into pure water at the exact same time, why would the calcium chloride vanish quickly while the sodium alginate remains clumpy?

Calcium chloride consists of small molecules that easily break apart into ions in water. Sodium alginate, however, is a massive polymer chain, meaning water molecules need much more time to physically work their way around the large, complex structure to dissolve it uniformly.

The Fabrication Process: Engineering the Beads

Now that we understand our materials, how do we engineer them into a drug delivery vehicle? We will follow a four-step process.

Step 1: Preparing the Solution and Loading the Drug

Because sodium alginate is so difficult to dissolve, I have pre-prepared the matrix solution for you. But a drug delivery particle isn’t very useful without a drug! Today, we will use food coloring as our "mock drug."

When you add a drop of the dye to the thick alginate solution, you will notice it doesn’t mix instantly. The dye sits on top and slowly diffuses downward. The thick polymer matrix physically hinders the dye molecules, forcing them to move slowly. You have to wait a few minutes for diffusion to create a uniform mixture. In a real lab, this drug is totally customized—it could be a cancer therapeutic, an anti-inflammatory, or even DNA!

Step 2: Crosslinking and Encapsulation

Once our drug is loaded into the alginate, we need to turn this liquid solution into a solid bead. We do this by dropping the alginate mixture into our calcium chloride bath.

This is where the magic happens. The \text{Ca}^{2+} ions act like little bridges, grabbing onto multiple alginate polymer chains and locking them together. This process, called crosslinking, instantly turns our liquid droplet into a solid hydrogel bead, perfectly encapsulating the drug inside!

What exactly is the calcium chloride bath doing to the liquid alginate droplet to make it solid?

The calcium ions (\text{Ca}^{2+}) from the bath act as little bridges that grab onto multiple alginate polymer chains at once. This chemical locking process, known as crosslinking, instantly binds the chains together to form a solid shell that traps the drug inside.

Hands-On: Forming and Measuring the Beads

Now it is your turn to get your hands dirty. You have a syringe, a dropper, your drug-loaded alginate, and a petri dish filled with about 10 to 20 milliliters of the calcium chloride bath.

As you do this, I want you to explore a critical engineering question: What factors affect the size and shape of the particle you get?

Try changing the height of your syringe. What happens if you drop it from high up versus holding it right near the surface? What happens if you push the plunger really fast instead of slowly?

Some of you are making beads with long "tails," or even long noodle-like structures! While we usually aim for perfect spheres, think about whether a special shape might be useful. Could a star-shaped or heart-shaped particle make taking medicine less intimidating for a child? Customizing the shape is a very real direction in nanomedicine research.

Once you have formed your beads, let them sit in the bath for about a minute to ensure the calcium fully crosslinks the outer shell, then scoop them out using your coffee filter.

How small can you make them? If you use the standard dropper, you might get beads that are 2 or 3 millimeters in diameter. But what if we change the opening size of the dropper?

As you can see, the opening size directly dictates the bead size. If you use a fine needle tip and apply very gentle pressure, you can produce incredibly tiny beads. In a professional research lab, we use specialized equipment to scale this exact same concept down to the true nanoscale, using real phospholipids and real genetic material.

Controlled Release: Physics in Action

Let’s take a moment to review the incredible process we just completed.

We have our beads, and they are loaded with our drug. But how does the drug actually get out of the solid bead and into the patient’s body? The underlying physical mechanism is passive diffusion.

Because of time constraints in today’s lab, we can’t sit and watch the release for hours. However, I ran this exact experiment before class so we could see the results.

Imagine you have two patients. One takes a "free drug" (just drinking the dye solution directly). The drug disperses into their body immediately. The other patient takes our engineered nanomedicine beads.

After 5 hours, the beads have slowly released the dye into the water. The beads themselves look almost transparent now, but they still hold a little bit of the drug. This is the power of a sustainable release platform!

Why does this matter so much? Beyond just maintaining a steady dosage, we can engineer these particles to be "smart." For example, tumor cells often have a lower pH (more acidic) than normal, healthy cells. We can design our polymer matrix to be pH-sensitive, meaning it stays locked tight in normal tissue but breaks open to release the cancer drug only when it encounters the acidic environment of a tumor. This ensures the drug attacks the disease without harming the healthy cells.

How could we use the concept of controlled release to treat a tumor without causing severe side effects to the rest of the patient’s healthy body?

We can engineer the nanoparticle matrix to be pH-sensitive so that it only breaks open in acidic environments. Since tumors typically have a lower pH than healthy tissue, the particle will hold onto the drug while traveling safely through the body and only release its payload once it reaches the tumor.

By simply playing with seaweed extract, salt water, and food coloring today, you have explored the fundamental chemistry, physics, and engineering that drives cutting-edge nanomedicine. Great job today, everyone! Please dispose of your liquids in the designated beakers and leave your vials on the bench. See you next time when we dive into nanoscale diagnostics!
